report.tagline: A UK company that designs the brain of almost every smartphone chip and earns a fee on each chip made with its designs.
report.simpleSummary: Arm does not usually make chips. It designs the blueprint for the processor, the part of a chip that does the thinking, and lets companies like Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek and Google use it. They pay Arm once to use the blueprint and then a small fee for every chip they sell. Since almost every phone in the world runs on Arm designs, those small fees add up to billions. In 2026 Arm also started selling its own complete server chip, called the AGI CPU.

overview.whatItDoes: Arm designs CPU architectures and ready-made processor cores. Chip companies license these designs and build them into their own chips for phones, laptops, cars, servers and smart devices. Arm earns an upfront licence fee and then a royalty on every chip shipped. Arm is about 90% owned by SoftBank and listed on Nasdaq.
howItWorks: Arm creates an instruction set architecture: the basic language a processor understands. The current version is Armv9.
A chip company signs a licence. Some take ready-made cores like Cortex; a few, like Apple and Qualcomm, license the architecture and design their own cores.
Arm also sells Compute Subsystems (CSS): bigger, pre-tested building blocks that save customers time and pay Arm a higher royalty.
The customer designs and sells its chip, made by factories like TSMC.
For every chip shipped, the customer pays Arm a royalty, usually a small percentage of the chip price.
Software makers write apps for Arm once, and they run on billions of Arm-based devices, which keeps everyone on Arm.
overview.valueProposition: Chip makers get a proven, power-efficient processor design and a huge software ecosystem without spending years and billions building their own from scratch.

painPoints.pain: Designing a processor from scratch costs billions and takes years.
painPoints.howSolved: License ready-made Cortex cores or Compute Subsystems and focus on the rest of the chip.
Arm designs are known for doing more work per unit of power.

painPoints.pain: A new chip is useless without software.
painPoints.howSolved: Android, iOS and most apps already run on Arm, so new chips get a full software library on day one.

painPoints.pain: Data centers spend heavily on electricity for AI.
painPoints.howSolved: Arm-based server chips like Graviton and the AGI CPU use less power per task.

painPoints.pain: Smaller chip companies lack big design teams.
painPoints.howSolved: Compute Subsystems give them a pre-built, tested design.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Ready-made processor designs for phones, cars and devices.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Main product for most licensees; drives royalty volume.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Processor designs for servers and cloud.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Growth engine as cloud firms move away from Intel and AMD.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Pre-integrated blocks of cores, memory links and more, ready to drop into a chip.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Saves customers months and earns Arm a higher royalty.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Arm's own complete data center processor, launched in March 2026 and sold directly.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: A big shift from earning a small fee to selling a whole chip, with much more revenue per unit, but it competes with some customers.

coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Keeps developers and chip makers locked into Arm.

businessModel.summary: Arm makes money in three ways: upfront licence fees to use its designs, royalties on every chip shipped, and since 2026, selling its own AGI CPU chips.

revenueStreams.detail: Upfront and subscription fees to use Arm designs, including Arm Total Access deals. $773 million in Jul to Sep 2026.
A fee per chip shipped, usually a small share of the chip price. $670 million in Jul to Sep 2026, up 8%.
Selling complete server processors. Arm expects about $2 billion across FY27 and FY28.

businessModel.pricing: Not public. Licence fees are negotiated per deal. Royalty rates are often reported at around 1% to 5% of chip price, higher for Armv9 and Compute Subsystems.
costDrivers: Engineers who design processors (the biggest cost)
For the AGI CPU: buying chips from factories, which brings real manufacturing costs
Legal costs, including the long fight with Qualcomm
businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough example: a $40 phone chip on Armv9 might pay Arm a royalty of about $0.50 to $1.50. That sounds tiny, but Arm's cost to collect it is almost zero, because the design work was already paid for. Multiply by billions of chips a year and most of that money is profit. Licensing fees cover a lot of the design cost upfront. The AGI CPU changes the maths: Arm might earn thousands of dollars per server chip, but it must pay the factory, so the margin per dollar is much lower than royalties.

howTheyGetUsers: Being the default design for phones, so new chip makers start with Arm
Selling to cloud giants that want lower power servers
Pushing into Windows laptops with Qualcomm and others
Offering Compute Subsystems to make Arm easier for smaller firms
Partnerships with software makers so their code runs best on Arm
whatBringsUsersBack: Each new chip generation needs a new licence
Royalties come every time a chip ships, for years
Software built for Arm makes switching to another design painful
Higher-value Armv9 and CSS upgrades for each new product
growth.moat: Arm's moat is the network effect of software. Billions of devices and almost every mobile app already run on Arm, so a chip maker that leaves Arm also leaves that software. The open RISC-V design is free to use and is a slow-growing threat, but it would take years to build the same software base.

competitors.name: x86 (Intel and AMD)
competitors.positioning: The traditional design for PCs and servers.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Arm wins on power use and licenses designs to anyone, while Intel and AMD sell their own chips.

competitors.name: RISC-V
competitors.positioning: A free, open instruction set anyone can use without royalties.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Arm has a far bigger software base and tested designs, but RISC-V is cheaper and gaining in China, cars and small devices.

competitors.name: Qualcomm's own Oryon cores
competitors.positioning: Custom cores built on an Arm architecture licence.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Arm earns less from custom cores than from its own designs, and the two companies have fought in court over licence terms.

competitors.name: Nvidia
competitors.positioning: AI chip leader that uses Arm cores in Grace CPUs.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Nvidia is a big customer, but Arm's AGI CPU now competes with server chips like Grace.

pmLessons: A platform can earn small amounts on huge volume. A dollar per chip on billions of chips is a big, high-margin business.
The real moat is often the ecosystem, not the technology. Software built for Arm keeps customers from leaving.
Moving into your customers' market can grow revenue but can also break trust. Every platform must weigh this.
Value-based pricing works: Arm earns more by selling more complete, more useful building blocks.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Arm sell its own chips, or stick to licensing?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare revenue per chip, margins and customer trust. Look at which markets have no conflict. Use metrics like licensee churn and AGI CPU margin.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you respond to the growth of RISC-V?
interviewQuestions.hint: Identify where RISC-V wins (cost, China, small devices). Propose cheaper entry plans and stronger software tools. Track new licences.

interviewQuestions.question: Royalty revenue grew only 8% last quarter. What would you investigate?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split by phones, cloud, cars and PCs. Check unit volumes, royalty per chip, timing of customer shipments, and the Qualcomm ruling.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Arm's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Chips shipped weighted by royalty value. Break into volume, royalty per chip, licensing pipeline and own-chip sales.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you price Compute Subsystems?
interviewQuestions.hint: Value-based: time saved and performance gained for the customer. Consider upfront fee vs higher royalty, and the risk of pushing customers away.
